title: Lesson 21: Low-Risk Ways to Start Automating, and When to Stop
description: Choosing the rare steps safe to hand over: the reversible-versus-irreversible filter, blast radius measured per task, and the warning signs that you have automated too much.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Low-Risk Ways to Start Automating, and When to Stop", what one rule carries the lesson?
options: Automate the reversible, keep the human on the irreversible
Automate the most frequent task first, whatever its reversibility
Automate everything at once and review the output weekly
Never automate any step that produces an email
questions.explanation: The lesson presents that sentence as the whole filter and says almost every low-risk decision follows from it, promoting steps one at a time and demoting them just as freely.

questions.question: How does the lesson define blast radius?
options: The number of teammates using the same tool
How much damage a wrong output can do, which belongs to the task rather than the tool
The size of the context window the task requires
The cost of the model call for the step
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts a wrong draft of a status summary with a wrong figure sent to fifty people and says the same tool can have a tiny radius on one task and a huge one on another.

questions.question: How does the lesson distinguish a workflow from automation?
options: Automation always requires writing code, while a workflow does not
A workflow runs on a schedule and automation runs on demand
In a workflow you are always at the check, while automation is a step that runs and checks itself, with you verifying less often or not at all
A workflow cannot draw on saved prompts
questions.explanation: The lesson states the difference is where your attention has to go: a workflow waits for you at the check, while automation is a step you deliberately promote from human-in-the-loop so the check can be left.
